zh: a[i] + a[i] ≠ 0 说明不能出现 0，a[i] + a[j] ≠ 0 说明不能同时有 x 和 −x；再加上互不相同，n 个数的绝对值必须是 n 个不同的正整数，所以最大绝对值至少是 n，而 1..n 恰好能达到这个下界。
看剩余元素中绝对值最大的那个：它为负时与所有剩余元素相加都为负，剩余正和计数为 0；为正时与所有剩余元素相加都为正，计数等于剩余个数 k（包括自己）。已确定的更大的正数会给每个剩余元素统一加上 offset 个正和。
把下标按 p 升序排序，用左右指针维护未处理的区间，剩余 k 从 n 递减。若最小的 p 等于 offset，就把它设为 −k；否则若最大的 p 等于 offset + k，就设为 +k 并让 offset 加一；两者都不成立或有 p 超出 [offset, offset+k] 就输出 None。p 可能是极长的十进制数，先按位数与 n 比较，超过 n 直接无解。
en: a[i] + a[i] != 0 rules out 0, and a[i] + a[j] != 0 rules out having both x and -x; together with distinctness, the n absolute values must be n different positive integers, so the largest absolute value is at least n, and using 1..n meets that bound.

Look at the remaining element with the largest absolute value: if it is negative, its sum with every remaining element is negative, so its remaining count is 0; if it is positive, every such sum is positive, so its count equals the number k of remaining elements (itself included). Already placed larger positive numbers add the same offset to every remaining element's count.

Sort the indices by p, keep left and right pointers over the unprocessed range, and let k go from n down to 1. If the smallest p equals offset, assign -k to it; otherwise if the largest p equals offset + k, assign +k and increase offset; if neither holds, or some p lies outside [offset, offset + k], print None. p may be a huge decimal string, so compare its digit count with n first and treat anything above n as impossible.

explanationEn:
## Source and conventions

The file fastprep/Codeium/codeium-erics-sequence.md at the fixed commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc fully specifies 1<=n<=100000, that p is a sequence of non-negative integers, and that p[i] counts the j for which a[i]+a[j]>0. j includes i itself. The elements of a must be pairwise distinct, and no two elements (including an element with itself) may sum to 0; among feasible solutions minimize the maximum absolute value, return any one when there are several, and return None when there is none. The catalog was truncated at an HTML comparison symbol, but the original rules and the range of n are not missing.

No numeric upper bound is given for p, and this site did not add an input restriction p<=n. p>n is a legal input but is necessarily infeasible; the program compares it with n directly by the number of decimal digits and lexicographic order, without converting very long numbers into machine integers. Decimal leading zeros are allowed, and very long leading zeros do not mean the value is out of range. This site only rearranged the original function's array input and output into text; the original has no examples, and all public examples were added by this site. No upstream code was executed.

## Approach

Sort the indices by p in ascending order and maintain the left and right ends of the part not yet assigned. Suppose k elements remain unprocessed and offset positive numbers have already been assigned. Their absolute values are larger than every value assigned later, so each of them contributes exactly one positive sum to every unprocessed element.

If the remaining element with the largest absolute value is negative, its remaining positive-sum count must be 0; if it is positive, its remaining count must be k (including itself). Therefore, when the current smallest p equals offset, assign -k to that index; otherwise, if the largest p equals offset+k, assign +k to that index and increase offset; if neither holds, there is no solution. Any p outside [offset, offset+k] also means there is no solution immediately. Each step decreases k by one.

## Proof of correctness

A valid solution cannot contain 0 (it would sum to 0 with itself), nor contain both x and -x; together with distinctness, all absolute values must be n different positive integers. Therefore the maximum absolute value is at least n.

In any valid remaining solution, the element with the largest absolute value has a negative sum with every remaining element if it is negative, and a positive sum with every remaining element if it is positive, so the remaining counts must contain 0 or k. The peeled positive numbers contribute offset uniformly, so the original counts must contain offset or offset+k. This proves that no valid solution exists when the algorithm fails.

Conversely, if an element with remaining count 0 exists, its sums with all remaining elements should be negative; setting it to -k and keeping all later absolute values below k satisfies both its own count and its zero contribution to the other elements. If an element has remaining count k, setting it to +k makes its sums with all remaining elements positive while contributing 1 uniformly to the others, so offset increases by 1. Removing this element yields a smaller problem of the same kind. The count bounds of all intermediate states must also be valid. By induction on the number of remaining elements, completing the whole peeling constructs a real witness that satisfies every p.

Each step uses a different absolute value k, so the final absolute values are exactly 1 to n, which satisfies distinctness and the zero-sum ban, and the maximum absolute value is exactly n, matching the lower bound above. Hence the construction is both feasible and globally optimal. Indices with equal p in the sort are interchangeable, and a unique answer is not required.

## Complexity and semantic judging

Let B be the total number of input characters. Reading and classifying very long decimal numbers takes O(B), sorting O(n log n), peeling O(n), and auxiliary space O(B+n). No arbitrary-precision arithmetic on the unbounded p is needed.

The dedicated checker does not require the same arrangement as the reference. It checks that the output contains exactly n integers whose absolute values are exactly 1..n, then sorts the output and uses binary search to count each element's positive sums, including itself. When the output is None, it checks feasibility independently. Different optimal arrangements all pass; scaling all values up does not change the positive-sum counts but breaks optimality, so it is rejected.

## Independent verification

A small oracle exhaustively tries all permutations of the absolute values 1..n with all sign choices and computes the positive-sum counts directly with a double loop, building a feasible witness for each count vector; it does not use sorting or peeling. Its 163 unique small inputs include feasible ones, infeasible ones, and p>n. They pass through subprocess runs of the real reference program and the independent witness check. The full n=100000 tests include all positive, all negative, shuffled mixed signs and impossible counts; inputs p for legal witnesses are generated by sorting and binary search. There are also tests with p of 100000 digits, very long leading zeros and a huge number at the end, all without shrinking the value domain. Two negative controls exit normally: one wrongly always prints None, and one doubles the optimal witness.
